source.title: The Signs Were Always There: Training-Free Detection and Control in Raw Transformer Dimensions
source.authors: V. Nalagatla; Madhavi Evana; Yi-Wen Zhang

page_placements.theme: Dense structure, anisotropy and privileged representation bases
Supervised subspaces and alternative functional units

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper explicitly replicates Elhage et al.’s toy autoencoder and measures feature sharing, geometric interference, and sign-based decoding in that toy setting.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the toy-model superposition measurements and the SAE feature-detection comparisons. The paper also reports many detection, safety, steering, and cross-modal results that do not test these claim versions. Sign-only reconstruction results are omitted because reconstruction quality does not by itself measure feature geometry or whether the represented features are one-dimensional.
record.test_reason: Appendix G replicates the Elhage et al. toy autoencoder and measures superposition on Elhage's own criteria: represented feature count against the bottleneck, ΣDi, features per dimension and mean |cos| between feature columns, at d=5 and d=20. That bears directly on V1. The LLM parts (Gemma SAE comparison, sign MI, probe ablation) benchmark the authors' BoD method or measure per-dimension sign coupling. They do not measure whether features are spread across neurons or whether SAE features are canonical, so V4–V6 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors replicate toy superposition on Elhage's criteria and explicitly say they do not refute superposition. They show per-dimension sign matching decodes the toy's features as well as projection, and that coupling and interference weaken as the bottleneck relaxes. They argue real transformers lack the toy's coupling signatures, so their capacity is combinatorial via sign patterns rather than geometric, and the high-pressure regime 'does not appear to be' where real models operate.
record.recipe_differences: Replicates Elhage et al.’s toy autoencoder, then adds per-dimension sign decoding, sign mutual information, and sign-only reconstruction analyses; the reported toy results use seed 42.
record.method_sensitivity: The toy measurements vary with sparsity and bottleneck width: d=5 settings have mean |cos| 0.333 and mean sign MI 0.0427–0.0708 bits; d=20 settings have mean |cos| 0.052–0.068 and mean sign MI 0.0056–0.0063 bits. SAE comparison performance varies with feature budget k.

fits_no_version.finding: Toy sign-MI between hidden dimensions is 0.043–0.071 bits at d=5 and falls to 0.0056–0.0063 bits at d=20. The authors compare this with real transformers at 0.0003–0.0036 bits (Table 22), where an MLP adds nothing over axis-aligned logistic regression.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The cross-dimension coupling seen in toy superposition depends on bottleneck pressure. Real transformers show weak coupling, with per-dimension sign features that are axis-aligned.

fits_no_version.finding: A training-free sign dictionary built from the unembedding retains 92–100% of a Gemma Scope SAE's above-chance sparse-probing accuracy and reaches parity at k=50.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse dictionary-like concept readouts in LLMs can be obtained without a learned rotation.

record.problems: The toy replication reports seed 42 and no uncertainty intervals for its configuration-level measurements. The SAE comparisons are limited to Gemma 3-4B and selected datasets; the paper says four of eight sparse-probing datasets were run. The toy results do not test feature importance or establish a general regular geometry.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying claim-related results were omitted from the selected toy geometry/decoding metrics or the reported SAE feature-detection tables. Other paper results, including random-initialization controls and language-model sign-feature analyses, were not included because they do not directly measure a version’s named claim object.

untested.parts: Sparsity-dependent transition: sparsity and n co-vary with a single seed, so no phase transition is mapped. Regular geometry (polytopes, digons, etc.) and feature-importance effects are not examined.
Not tested. Importance-driven dedicated dimensions are not measured. The text only notes the 1/Di spread widens at d=20.

Not tested. The SAE results are benchmarks of BoD. Sign-MI and probe-ablation results bear on cross-dimension coupling, not on whether features are distributed across neurons or recoverable by a dictionary.
Not tested. BoD matching the SAE does not test completeness, stability or canonicity of SAE features.
Not tested. No measurement of feature dimensionality.

missing.what: At d=20 the spread of 1/Di widens from 2.9–4.1 to 1.0–8.4, so some features get an almost dedicated dimension.

Real-transformer pairwise sign MI (0.0003–0.0036 bits mean) and the MLP-vs-LogReg probe ablation (MLP never better). These are the authors' basis for saying real models are not in the toy's pressure regime.
missing.locator: Appendix N Table 22; Appendix C Table 8

record.verdict_notes: Toy results use a single seed with no uncertainty. Sparsity is confounded with n. The SAE comparison rows benchmark the study's own method and were unlinked. V6 links were removed because sign decoding says nothing about feature dimensionality. No embedded instructions found.

versions.untested_parts: The toy experiments vary sparsity and bottleneck width, but do not test feature importance or establish a general regular geometric arrangement.
The study does not test whether neuron polysemanticity results from capacity competition, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
The study does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.

SAE feature detection is benchmarked on Gemma 3-4B for selected datasets and sites. The paper does not directly establish that LLM features are distributed across neurons, or test the claim across a broad range of LLMs and SAE designs.
The study compares SAE and BoD performance, but does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
The toy experiments use feature columns/directions and compare sign decoding with projection onto those directions. The study does not establish the geometric dimensionality of features in real LLMs.
